title: A Scandal at the Center of the Economy
summary: Given the obsession over the AI race between the United States and China, you might imagine that news of the man leading the most important company in AI being caught in an extramarital relationship with a woman believed to be a Chinese spy would spark outrage and excoriation without parallel. You c...
content:
Given the obsession over the AI race between the United States and China, you might imagine that news of the man leading the most important company in AI being caught in an extramarital relationship with a woman believed to be a Chinese spy would spark outrage and excoriation without parallel. You could suppose that such reckless behavior, upon discovery, might lead to widespread calls for immediate resignation and for deep investigation—not just of the executive, but the entire company. Pitchforks, et cetera.

It is curious, then, that, as news came out that the Nvidia CEO, Jensen Huang, had had a romantic relationship with a Chinese businesswoman who was also an asset of Beijing’s Ministry of State Security, notable factions of Silicon Valley and Washington, D.C., seemed nonplussed. “Even incredible humans make mistakes,” Bill Ackman, the billionaire hedge-fund manager, posted on X yesterday. “We should all support him and his family. Onward.” The venture capitalist Shaun Maguire offered a five-point analysis of Huang’s situation, noting that the CEO did something “incredibly dumb” and “bad for America,” but that “my guess is there was no bad intention.” He then argued, “I believe Jensen is irreplaceable for America’s AI leadership.” Elon Musk agreed. From there, the posts, written before we know all the facts of the scandal, got only more absurd, including defending Huang’s affair on the grounds that his kids are adults now.

[Read: America can’t afford an AI recession]

Later in the day, Donald Trump echoed calls for Huang to stay on as CEO. He called Huang “an honorable guy.” The president, who has had extramarital affairs of his own and is credibly accused of sexual crimes by numerous women, sounded unbothered. “I think he probably has an excuse for it,” Trump added. Nvidia’s board of directors seemed equally deferential. It announced an independent investigation into the incident but also stressed that it has “no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised” and that it “has confidence in Jensen and his leadership team.” Huang, for his part, issued a statement yesterday acknowledging the affair and noting that he would cooperate with the investigation.

It’s tempting to see this as little more than powerful men defending their kind—a classic example of bros before pressing technological-geopolitical security imperatives. But that explanation misses both Huang’s and Nvidia’s centrality in American politics and the global financial system. Nvidia’s chips are arguably the most important infrastructure component of the AI boom; without the tech, the OpenAIs and Anthropics of the world would be unable to train or power their models—reporting suggests that billionaires have begged Huang for greater allocations of Nvidia chips. This intense demand has made Nvidia a financial juggernaut; in May, its market capitalization was $5.7 trillion, which made it larger than every economy except that of the U.S. and China.

Last year, my colleague Matteo Wong and I described the U.S. as an Nvidia-state, much like Saudi Arabia is a petrostate. That’s because, in recent years, the company has become one of the biggest investors of other AI companies; As of July, Nvidia announced that its equity investments valued roughly $99 billion, including in companies such as OpenAI, Anthropic, SpaceX, and data-center providers like CoreWeave. It’s a circular style of investment where companies pay Nvidia enormous sums of money for its chips and then Nvidia reinvests some of that money back into those companies and their competitors, in part so that they can continue to buy chips. You could make a strong case that Nvidia helps support big chunks of the Magnificent Seven ecosystem, the tech companies that are responsible for roughly a third of the S&P 500’s current value. According to The Economist, Nvidia stock has produced “15 cents of every dollar the American stock market has returned since 2023.”

Huang, who founded Nvidia in 1993, is the company’s key figure, praised by many in the tech industry as one of the visionaries responsible for the rapid acceleration of artificial intelligence. He’s instrumental in the company’s engineering decisions, its allocation of chips, and other investments. He also has no clear successor. Outside of Silicon Valley, Huang has become a trusted adviser and ally to Trump on AI policy. Huang’s thinking on issues such as AI doomerism (he’s anti-doom) and chip allocation in China (he’s for it—a position that warrants examining, given this weekend’s revelations) influences U.S. policy. This centrality is why one tech analyst on CNBC this morning implied that replacing Huang was a comical suggestion. Huang is a singular figure: the linchpin of the company that is arguably the linchpin of the American economy. Framed another way, Nvidia has much of the financial system in a hostage situation. Huang is too big to fail. Which may be why so many people seem motivated to downplay or protect him right now.

How else would one describe the prolific excuse-making for him? The information that has come out around Huang’s involvement with the alleged Chinese spy is alarming. Concerns about the relationship have been mounting for more than a year. Alice Huang (no relation to Jensen) worked for the Singaporean data-center company Megaspeed, an Nvidia client the government had been investigating regarding its potential connections to the Chinese government. As The New York Times reported today, Nvidia intervened in the U.S. Department of Commerce’s investigation of Megaspeed; the probe was subsequently halted and transferred to the Justice Department. According to the Times, Trump was briefed about Huang’s relationship roughly a year ago, including the presumption that Alice may be a spy, and “chose not to do anything with that intelligence.”

In recent weeks, the Nvidia spokesperson John Rizzo and Huang himself both dismissed claims that the relationship with the woman in question was unusual or romantic in any way—we now know this was untrue. It’s still unclear whether Huang disclosed any pertinent corporate or national-security secrets or whether his relationship with an alleged spy had any impact on Nvidia’s opposition to semiconductor export controls in China. But everything we know so far paints Huang, Nvidia, and government officials in a terrible light, at every turn either ignoring or obfuscating a national-security problem.

As more information about the relationship comes out, lawmakers will have to choose whether to take their cues from the markets (Nvidia shares dropped 8.8 percent at one point today—a $400 billion drop in the company’s valuation) or push for more investigation. Trump, who has been reliably motivated in his presidency by the stock market, seems indebted to Nvidia’s performance in the market, as well as to AI investment in general. He’s unlikely to do anything to jeopardize that. Democrats are in a particularly interesting position, fresh off a midterm rout centered on taking a strong stance against tech oligarchs, AI, and data centers and in favor of corporate accountability. Earlier today, Senator Chris Coons said on X that he would push for an investigation into Huang and Nvidia. To press hard on Huang to resign, or to dig deeper into what he and the company knew about the relationship and when, will inevitably risk adding volatility to Nvidia’s share price and, by virtue, the larger Gordian knot of AI investment that is predicated on relentless growth and continued scale. All of this is to say that the moral case regarding Huang is much different from the one that Trump and those with a financial interest in Nvidia’s success will likely consider.

This scandal holds an irony that’s especially befitting of the AI moment. Huang seemingly has cozied up to his industry’s No. 1 foe, China, the boogeyman that, by the professed logic of Silicon Valley’s AI executives, is forcing many of his peers to build a product that they fear. Instead of denouncing him, Washington and Silicon Valley are motivated to circle the wagons around Huang, in part because doing so keeps the system moving and the money flowing. The build at all costs rationale that dictates treating China’s AI prowess as an existential threat is also driving the same people to brush past an egregious dalliance with that enemy.

This is the type of warped incentives that the AI race produces. Playing the game necessitates embracing preposterous risk to justify an idealized future outcome. To run this race requires its participants to withstand intense cognitive dissonance and behave in ways that make them appear ever more inscrutable and reckless to those who are not involved. If nothing else, Huang is a useful example to understand what happens when the fortunes of countries and many of its most powerful citizens are all tied up in one progressively intricate technological and financial bet. In this way, Huang is the AI boom personified, a hyperobject of a man who has wound his way into the center of the economy and whose influence, depending on how you look at it, may usher in either prosperity or untold doom.

title: The End of Stephen Miller’s Recusals
summary: Stephen Miller spent his first weekend as White House chief of staff on the patio at Mar-a-Lago, huddling with President Trump and Natalie Harp, his executive assistant, about how to approach the next two years with the House and Senate under Democratic control. Katie Miller—the podcaster, political...
content:
Stephen Miller spent his first weekend as White House chief of staff on the patio at Mar-a-Lago, huddling with President Trump and Natalie Harp, his executive assistant, about how to approach the next two years with the House and Senate under Democratic control. Katie Miller—the podcaster, political consultant, and wife of Stephen—spent the weekend in the Washington area, rearranging her own life. “I make every decision based on what’s best for my children and our family,” she wrote yesterday on X, before announcing that she had decided to wind down her podcast.

But that was not all that was changing. For months, Stephen Miller has recused himself from matters of policy that involve Katie Miller’s other financial interests at the direction of the White House counsel. That meant that Stephen did not work on issues involving the media company Paramount, where his wife had been seeking a podcast deal, or anything to do with space policy or artificial intelligence, because his wife, a longtime adviser to Elon Musk, also worked for SpaceX, the owner of the Grok artificial-intelligence assistant. All of that changed today.

Katie Miller severed her employment with SpaceX, sold her stock in the company, and forfeited her right to future equity that had not yet vested under her contract, according to a person familiar with the moves. Over the weekend, she also ended a separate contract with Paramount for a planned podcast deal. As a result, a White House official told me this afternoon, “Stephen Miller is no longer subject to any recusals and may fully participate in all meetings and policy matters.” Katie declined to comment.

White House lawyers had previously ruled that Katie Miller’s podcast advertising sponsorships from companies seeking official favor from her husband did not require recusals, because sponsorships carry a different ethical significance than consulting arrangements. Sugar-soda boosters at the American Beverage Association, the utility Southern Company, and the Merchants Payments Coalition, a group pushing for legislation to reduce credit-card swipe fees, had all purchased time on her show. But now even those potential conflicts will not be an issue, after a couple more already-recorded episodes from her podcast are released. “Nothing is more important than raising our four kids,” she wrote. “While I’ve loved the podcast, the time commitment is too great and now is the time to step away.”

[Read: A chief of staff who ‘will crack skulls’]

The Millers met during the first Trump term, when both were working for the administration. Katie Miller later worked as a press secretary and communications director for Vice President Pence, before becoming an adviser to Musk, the founder of SpaceX and CEO of Tesla. During the transition following the 2024 presidential election, Katie Miller worked as an adviser to future Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., before joining the White House as a special government employee who advised Musk and the Department of Government Efficiency. When she left the White House, she maintained her consulting work for Musk and SpaceX, leading the White House counsel to advise that Stephen Miller recuse himself on related issues. When Katie Miller began working closely with Paramount, offering to help arrange a company party for Trump before the White House Correspondents’ Dinner, Stephen Miller expanded his recusals to cover related issues.

Katie Miller’s career change comes amid a public uproar over possible improper influence in the White House, after the former adviser Calley Means went on Joe Rogan’s podcast to allege “demonic” efforts to influence White House policy by lobbyists with close ties to senior officials. Concern about corruption, often focused on the president’s own for-profit efforts in office and the business deals of his children, became a significant issue in the recent midterm elections. Gallup found in September that 89 percent of U.S. adults believed that corruption was widespread in the government, a proportion that had risen 10 points in just one year to the highest level in the two decades that the polling question had been asked.

After Trump announced his new chief of staff on Friday afternoon, Katie Miller responded on X: “Watching your best friend and spouse achieve their dreams is a once-in-a-lifetime experience.” She kept the commentary going through the weekend. When Politico published an article about how she had lobbied for the promotion, Miller responded: “BREAKING: Wife supports husband. If your wife doesn’t do this, find a new one.”

title: The Inconvenient Truth at the Center of the Immigration Debate
summary: Have liberals learned anything from the border crisis that helped return Donald Trump to office two years ago? Many have not, if a recent report from the American Civil Liberties Union is any indication. The group claims to offer a “way forward” for the country’s asylum system, which has become a ba...
content:
Have liberals learned anything from the border crisis that helped return Donald Trump to office two years ago? Many have not, if a recent report from the American Civil Liberties Union is any indication. The group claims to offer a “way forward” for the country’s asylum system, which has become a back door for economic migrants. But the ACLU instead recycles arguments that immigration advocates have made for decades. Too many progressives fail to understand, or acknowledge, the real reason migrants, including those intending to seek asylum, cross the border illegally: People come when they think they can stay.

I have been working on border and immigration policy for more than 20 years, serving in senior roles at the White House and the Department of Homeland Security as well as Senate staff. I have seen, up close, surges in illegal immigration under both Democratic and Republican presidents. Again and again, the loudest and most extreme voices have set the immigration agenda for each party, to the detriment of the country. Despite Trump’s concession in yesterday’s 60 Minutes interview that his administration’s handling of immigration was “too tough,” his elevation of the anti-immigration hard-liner Stephen Miller as his chief of staff suggests that this trend will continue. Immigration advocates who deplore the Trump administration’s aggressive tactics have an obligation to propose realistic, constructive alternatives.

Yet on the left, the ACLU and other immigration advocates continue to argue that enforcement at the border, including restrictions on asylum eligibility, do not prevent or deter illegal immigration; they simply create pent-up demand and encourage migrants to attempt more dangerous routes. As a result, according to advocacy groups, the only way to stem the tide of illegal immigration is to address the underlying problems that push people to leave their countries, and to provide more legal pathways for these migrants to come to the United States.

[From the November 2026 issue: The babies left behind in America]

In reality, the United States’ inability to promptly remove those who lack a legal basis to remain in the country has been the driving force behind every major surge in illegal immigration since the Obama administration.

The U.S. asylum system, created by Congress at the height of the Cold War, presumes that almost everyone who passes an initial screening deserves legal protection. As a result, more than 80 percent of people who claimed asylum at the border from 2014 to 2019 were released into the country, yet immigration judges ultimately granted asylum in less than a fifth of these cases. This legal process can take years, during which seekers are allowed to apply to work, which makes it easy for economic migrants to game the system. Nobody would spend $15,000 in smuggling fees and experience the mortal dangers of the journey north if they didn’t believe that they could stay and get a job.

Before 2011, only about 2 percent of people who crossed the border illegally claimed asylum. But as word got out that most people who claim asylum at the border are let in, the percentage of undocumented border crossers who claimed asylum steadily increased, to 16 percent in 2013 and then to 59 percent in 2023––far outstripping the U.S. government’s capacity to process applications in a timely manner.

The Obama administration experienced its first surge in migration from Central American families claiming asylum at the border. At the time, advocacy groups persuaded senior officials and key members of Congress to focus on the root causes of illegal immigration—such as violence, corruption, and political instability in other countries—instead of tackling the incentives in the asylum system that encouraged migrants to come here. In 2016, the U.S. invested a record $750 million in aid in projects to create jobs, enhance governance, and improve security in the region. The initiative made modest improvements, but could not fix the problems that were encouraging so many people to flee. What kept illegal border crossings at manageable levels on President Obama’s watch was an increase in border security, a more stringent enforcement of immigration laws within the country, and record-high deportation numbers—for which immigration advocates gave the president the not-so-flattering title of “Deporter-in-Chief.”

At the start of Trump’s first term, the new president’s tough talk about the “invasion” at the border seemed to have deterred some would-be migrants and so further reduced illegal crossings. But migrants soon realized that they could still game America’s asylum system. By 2019 Border Patrol apprehensions along the southwest border exceeded 850,000, up 115 percent from 2018. Trump’s initial response—to separate the families of asylum seekers at the border—was both ineffective at deterring migration and abhorrent to many Americans. Other restrictions on asylum that his administration introduced in 2019, such as the “Remain in Mexico” program that required asylum seekers to wait in Mexico as their cases played out in U.S. court, had inhumane consequences but did curb border crossings. Emergency measures during the coronavirus pandemic cut the number of crossings even more. But as the pandemic eased, people began moving north again.

When President Biden took office in January 2021, illegal crossings had already begun to surge, averaging 70,000 a month from October 2020 through his inauguration. Instead of addressing this problem, Biden spent his first days in office fulfilling campaign promises to immigration advocates. He announced a moratorium on deportations and ended Trump’s asylum restrictions, sending a clear message that the U.S. border was going to be open. He also put Vice President Harris in charge of a strategy to invest more than $5.2 billion in private-sector funds to create more economic opportunities in Central America, which once again did not reduce immigration from the region.

Another common argument among immigration advocates is that expanding access to legal immigration will take pressure off the border. The problem is that no realistic amount of legal pathways will satisfy global demand to immigrate to the United States. When I was in the Biden administration, we oversaw the largest expansion of lawful pathways for migrants in a generation, explicitly to reduce illegal immigration from Cuba, Haiti, Nicaragua, and Venezuela. What we found was that illegal crossings dropped only when they triggered clear consequences at the border, such as repatriation of ineligible asylum seekers to Mexico. The United States can and should increase legal pathways for immigrants, but the goal should be to enhance economic growth and reunite families—not to prevent illegal immigration.

There is a cruel irony in the fact that, by pushing policies that enable economic migrants to gain entry into the United States via the asylum system, human-rights advocates have encouraged migrants to put their lives at risk on their way to the U.S. border. In 2023, I was part of a delegation to Colombia and Panama to urge those governments to close the Darién Gap—a treacherous and sometimes lethal route between the two countries through which migrants trekked to the United States. From a helicopter, I saw thousands of people streaming out of the jungle after a week-long ordeal. On the ground, we met children who survived the journey but were alarmingly weak from exhaustion and dehydration. We learned that human-rights groups were providing migrants with supplies—including birth control for women, many of whom would be sexually assaulted by smugglers during the illegal crossing. I believe that none of those migrants would have risked these dangers if they didn’t think that the United States would let them stay.

[Read: The problem with shutting down ICE in blue states]

The Biden administration learned the hard way that the only reliable way to deter illegal immigration was to restrict asylum—such as by setting more stringent screening criteria and requiring asylum seekers to set up interview appointments in advance and use a designated port of entry—and increase resources to enforce these laws at the border. In 2023, these curbs on asylum-seeking worked initially, but encounters at the border with Mexico surged when enforcement by Mexican authorities waned, and fell sharply when this enforcement expanded in concert with U.S. efforts in early 2024. By mid-2024, when Biden introduced more asylum restrictions at the border, encounters dropped by roughly 55 percent—from about 120,000 in May to about 56,000 in July.

But by then, the perception that his party couldn’t or wouldn’t keep the border under control had helped doom Democrats’ prospects in the November election. Following the advice of immigration advocates when he took office and waiting too long to change course were among Biden’s biggest mistakes.

At least some progressive leaders seem keen to avoid these mistakes. “I think we’ve learned the lesson,” Michigan Senator-Elect Abdul El-Sayed said about the chaos at the border under Biden in a preelection 60 Minutes interview with Ross Douthat. “You can humanely enforce the border.”

Voters are plainly tired of the wild swings in policy between permissiveness and cruelty. The Trump administration’s poll numbers on immigration suggest that the president’s merciless approach to migrants—which led to the fatal shootings of people protesting enforcement actions—contributed to his party’s stunning electoral defeat last week. Trump promised a crackdown on the “worst of the worst.” Instead, his administration has redeployed federal resources that were once used to address and prevent more serious crimes, such as terrorism, fentanyl smuggling, and child sex trafficking, to deport otherwise law-abiding people in the United States.

The Trump administration has also waged an all-out war on legal immigration, rescinding the lawful status of about 1.8 million immigrants, restricting access to green cards, halting visa processing in mostly nonwhite countries, and cutting naturalizations of new U.S. citizens by 75 percent. This despite the warnings of economists that these policies would measurably harm economic growth. American agricultural producers now say that ICE’s indiscriminate raids are hurting domestic farmers and threaten to raise grocery prices even further.

Like Biden, Trump is listening too closely to the most radical voices in his coalition—and he has paid a political price for it. Every single congressional district on the U.S. border with Mexico is projected to be held by a Democrat next year. But his promotion of Miller, the architect of his cruel and nativist approach to immigration, suggests that he has not learned from this electoral rebuke.

Most Americans hold heterodox views on border and immigration policies: They want strong enforcement at the border, but they want this enforcement to be fair and humane, and for people who have otherwise lawfully contributed to their communities for years to be able to stay. Immigration policy shouldn’t be just the province of ACLU-style progressives and hard-liners such as Miller. Lawmakers should stop pandering to the extremes of their bases and step up to fix America’s broken immigration and asylum system once and for all.

title: Congress vs. Hegseth
summary: Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube | Overcast | Pocket CastsBack in February, when the United States and Israel first attacked Iran, President Trump said that it would be a “short-term excursion.” Now, eight months later, as the war with Iran remains without conclusion, the president...
content:
Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube | Overcast | Pocket Casts

Back in February, when the United States and Israel first attacked Iran, President Trump said that it would be a “short-term excursion.” Now, eight months later, as the war with Iran remains without conclusion, the president and his party are dealing with its consequences. As Vice President Vance put it last Tuesday, when Republicans were ousted from their seats in the House and the Senate—not to mention governor’s mansions and statehouses—in a fierce rebuke to the administration’s policies: “The reason we lost is the war.”

If voters swung Congress to Democrats in response to the war and its effects, what comes next? Democrats have said that they will vote to end the war; they’ve said, with some Republican support, that they will begin impeachment hearings for Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth. But after naming the hard-line adviser Stephen Miller, the architect and champion of some of the president’s most aggressive domestic and foreign policies, as his chief of staff, Trump may as well double-down on the agenda he’s chased for the past two years. This week on Radio Atlantic, our staff writers Nancy Youssef and Tom Nichols discuss where the administration goes from here, what options exist to get out of Iran, what to make of Hegseth’s potential impeachment, and how the Defense Secretary has changed the relationship between American democracy and the American military.


The following is a transcript of the episode:

Nancy Youssef: The most enduring impact [Pete] Hegseth has had, in addition to the war, is on personnel. These are people with 20, 30 years experience, and then there’s all the impacts you don’t see—the captains and the majors who are looking at what’s happened to those ahead of them and saying, I’m not gonna stick around. That’s years and years of investment that has been lost, and will take years and years and years to replace.

Adam Harris: This is Radio Atlantic. I’m Adam Harris, and today, we need to talk about the war in Iran.

Voters cared about the war in this election. An AP poll showed that seven in 10 registered voters wanted to see it end. After Democrats rode a blue wave back to power last Tuesday, Vice President J. D. Vance wrote on social media, “The reason we lost is the war.”

Now Democrats are exploring the legislative tools they have to act as a check on the administration: They have the War Powers Act, they could withhold military funds through appropriations. But as hard-line adviser Stephen Miller takes over as the new White House chief of staff and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth continues to enthusiastically defend his position and the war, the question remains: Where does the administration go from here in a war of their own making?

Joining me to discuss are my colleagues Nancy Youssef and Tom Nichols. Let’s get to questions.

Harris: Tom, welcome back to the show.

Tom Nichols: Thanks, Adam.

Harris: Nancy, great to see you.

Nancy Youssef: Great to be with you.

Harris: Nancy, right after the election, we saw Republicans across the spectrum jump to blaming Iran and the Iran war for their loss. Vice President J. D. Vance quickly tried to distance himself from the conflict, and then Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth released a video in support of the war, saying:

Pete Hegseth: Peace through strength is once again American military policy. Our commander in chief demands it, and so we deliver it.

Harris: What does his reaction tell us about the discord within the administration?

Youssef: Well, Pete Hegseth was the most vocal advocate of this war, not only internally within the administration, but publicly as well, arguing that this was a just fight, that the United States was stopping Iran from having a nuclear weapon—all without releasing key details about what precisely was happening on the ground or at what cost it was coming to the United States in terms of munitions.

And so I think the five-minute video was as much about Iran as it was about threats of an impeachment hearing that Tom Massie put forth before the last session, and Speaker [Mike] Johnson notably relieved Congress so that they wouldn’t have that hearing. There’s at least six charges, some of them related to the war as well as to the boat strikes and some of the other actions that the secretary’s taken.

Hegseth: A disgruntled, defeated congressman, along with all his Democrat allies has also dropped sham articles of impeachment against yours truly.

Youssef: And so in a weird way, the secretary’s sort of conceding that he faced impeachment by putting out this video and saying that the military needed to come to defense and fight the fight. He didn’t say exactly against whom, but there you go. But he launched a very forceful defense for an impeachment that hasn’t happened yet.

But I think more than anybody, he is personally tied to this war because of his advocacy for it. I think if you’re a legislator thinking about impeachment, that video also signaled what he will do if impeached, which is to try to use it as a form of leverage with the president and potentially for his future political career and say that he’s being targeted much in the same way that [Donald] Trump has felt that he got targeted with some of the previous impeachments against him.

And so the question becomes, I think, if you’re in Congress, is this the best way to do it, and is this the best time to do it, particularly if the impeachment itself might not lead to a conviction in the Senate?

Harris: Tom, we’re seeing this post-midterms shakeup. Stephen Miller is the new chief of staff. Pete Hegseth is under fire from Congress. What does the last week mean for what we can expect out of the White House after the midterms?

Nichols: Well, for one thing, the president’s already set the tone: It wasn’t my fault. Had I been on the ballot—which he was, in a way—we would’ve won these things. And so, there’s gonna be a lot of blame-storming going on.

Harris: I guess I should say too: What does it mean for the war in Iran? What does it mean for the White House strategy in the war with Iran?

Nichols: Well, for the war in Iran, that’s really hard to say because, in theory, Miller has told the president that they have to get out. But that requires Donald Trump admitting a mistake, giving a W to the regime in Tehran, because it will survive and just washing his hands of it.

So I suspect that, at least in the short term, it’s gonna be more of what we’re seeing now, that the president acts as if the war is pretty much over. In his interview with Ross Douthat, he said when Ross asked him, What about the strait being closed? And he said, But it’s open.

To which, you know, yes, it’s open because there are U.S. Navy ships right now staying there at great expense and a certain amount of risk.

And I suspect that you’ll have this kind of phony war going on, where it’s neither peace nor war but it’s to get it out of the public eye and somehow be able to claim what Trump has always wanted to claim. Since the first few weeks of the war, when regime change didn’t happen, what Trump’s really wanted is: Give me a way to say that I won so that I can get out of this thing. And of course that wasn’t helped—I mean, to bring it back to Pete Hegseth—it didn’t help that Pete Hegseth, at least until May, was going out there and saying: We’re killing it. We’re winning. We’re going gangbusters.

Important to note that it’s been now six months since the Defense Department has bothered to give a press briefing. And I think that’s what to expect from the war. That there will be stories about a strike here or there, kind of the way maybe—and it’s an imperfect analogy—but kind of the way that the second Iraq war kind of trailed off. You’d open the paper and say, Oh, we struck some targets in northern Iraq, or, Our planes were fired on as they flew over southern Iraq.

But I think that will suit the Iranians just fine. The president again was asked what is in the future, and he said, All those countries are gonna pay every penny that we’ve spent on this war. That’s not going to happen. So, who knows?

Harris: You mentioned the interview with Ross where he’s like, Well, the ships are passing through the strait. The strait is open. And he says it’s at great expense, and he’s like, Well, it’s not at great expense. Nancy, can you talk about the expense to this point of the war and what’s necessary in order to keep it over there, as it were?

Youssef: So the expense is that naval blockade, which is a very heavy military effort. It takes a number of ships. There are two aircraft-carrier groups in the region right now. There is talk of a third one joining in the coming weeks, the USS Theodore Roosevelt, which is currently near Singapore. When you have that many ships in the region, it means you cannot have naval assets in Europe, in Asia, in the area that Stephen Miller’s particularly interested in, the Western Hemisphere.

There just aren’t enough assets to have that kind of lift in the strait and do missions in other places. Moreover, it comes at great risk to not only the ships that are there because the Iranians are targeting them, but ground forces in the region as well, and we’ve seen that happen. And so we’ve seen an extra supplement of air defenses in the region and at the expense again of other parts in the region.

We see this, for example, in the inability of the United States to provide further munitions to Ukraine. The U.S. simply doesn’t have it. And remember, the Iranians are firing cheaply made drones and in some cases even ballistic missiles against the United States. It’s much more expensive, much more costly, much longer to resupply air defense capabilities like the THAAD and the Patriot.

So that’s sort of the immediate cost. But I think Tom’s point is an important one, in terms of where we are in the war.

I think right now we’re seeing sort of three options, in terms of what the president is trying to do. We heard him yesterday say that it was highly unlikely that the U.S. would go back to war, and I think he’s saying that for one of three reasons.

Either it’s a head fake and the United States is gonna resume strikes. Or he thinks it’s part of a negotiation tactic. Or he’s just saying it. But whatever it is, he has signaled he does not want to go back. The big change, though, for the Iranians, is twofold: One, Iran thinks that they have leverage in this conflict and don’t need to make any capitulations. And two, that midterm election has bolstered their confidence and their ability to negotiate.

And so while the president may try to kind of punt making this decision, at some point, both the cost of the blockade to the U.S. military and the Iranians’ unwillingness to hold this position or to stick to it will make that position untenable. There is a clock ticking in all this. And so while the president wants to keep it in the distance, at some point—I can’t tell you when or how—that will not be a sustainable position.

Harris: When we’re back, how the Democratic wins in the midterms might affect the path of the war.

[Break]

Harris: Nancy, Democrats now have an opportunity to do what they said they wanted to do: rein in the war. What are you all hearing now from Democrats, now that they’ve won the election, about possibilities for reining in the war?

Youssef: So I think a couple things. One is the impeachment hearing, because if you have an impeached secretary of defense, that certainly—even if he’s not convicted—that certainly puts a spotlight on the war itself. Because even if it’s not the only reason, it’s one of several reasons, and it requires a reexamination.

I think the second thing you’re hearing is questions about funding for the Pentagon. One of the problems that the Pentagon’s facing now is: It’s running out of funding. Hegseth is asking for $1.5 trillion, and we’ve heard bipartisan concern about that level of spending without getting any transparency, in terms of what’s happening in terms of the war.

Harris: How abnormal is that level of spending, $1.5 trillion?

Youssef: We’ve never had that. So usually, defense spending, if you were to make a chart, it kinda goes up and down. So World War II spikes, then it goes back down. Then it goes back up again for Korea, then goes back down. Then it goes up for Vietnam, then it goes back down.

And then after 9/11, it just steadily increased. And so what we’ve seen is a growing and growing defense budget. What’s interesting is that they’re talking about increasing defense spending while reducing the number of troops in Europe; while reducing the number of troops in the Middle East, potentially; while sort of focusing on this hemisphere, and yet asking for a larger defense budget.

So it’s not just the number, but it’s incongruent with what they’re saying they want to use the Pentagon for. And so they’re running low on funds as it is, and I think Hegseth might be a form of leverage that they try to use to say: If you want us to continue to approve funding, we need to see a change at the top.

The other thing I think you’re gonna see a push for is a lot more access to information that legislators and the public used to have about the conduct of war. We don’t know with any fidelity what the stockpile situation is in terms of munitions, what damage happened to the bases, how much it’ll cost to fix, which bases will be fixed, what that means for the future of U.S. military posture.

How do you continue to have naval forces in the Middle East when you’ve lost the basing access you need to restock those ships and have liberty visits for the troops? Very basic questions haven’t been answered. And I think one of the things you’ll see, if nothing else, is a push for more of that.

Now, whether they get it is something else because there’s been a real tension between the Hill and the secretary. But those answers, I think, are necessary to understand and really hold the department accountable for its conduct of the war. You can’t do it if you don’t have basic facts about what it’s done so far and at what cost.

Harris: Earlier this month, Military.com released a poll saying that 53 percent of active service members say they want to separate from the military sooner because the military is becoming more politicized.

This is a lot. Tom, how is the administration affecting this decline in morale among service members?

Nichols: From the first day of his first term, Donald Trump has attacked the traditions of American civil-military relations. All presidents have done—you know, when they show up at military academies or they go to a military base ostensibly for a nonpartisan event—all presidents skate that line every now and then because they like to have the military as kind of a backdrop to what they’re doing.

Donald Trump has left that line in the dirt miles behind him. He has tried actively to tell the military: You are a constituency of the Republican Party and of my support group personally. You are part of me, rather than America. And that hurts morale. I taught for 25 years at the Navy War College, and I taught hundreds of officers.

And they all have very—you know, these are men and women of strong political opinions. Have a drink at the O Club, the Officers’ Club, you’ll hear them. But in a way, they took great pride in what I always called the “miracle” of American civil-military relations, which is that we are the most powerful military in the world, and yet no threat to our democracy whatsoever.

I think people don’t realize how amazing that is: that a massively powerful military that is absolutely contained within the democratic structure of a large and vibrant and diverse country. And I think that, for many of them, the military is a refuge from politics; that when they go to work and they fly a helicopter or, they’re leading PT, whatever they’re doing, it’s not political.

They’re one organization, one mission. And Donald Trump has really divided them about that. And when you start introducing that suspicion—about promotions, about people kind of getting the side eye because of something you might have said—that turns us into a Soviet military, not an American military. That turns us into a Third World military. And that serves Donald Trump’s purposes just fine because, again, he wants the military to be actively engaged in politics.

I wrote a piece a while back where I was sort of desperately yelling for somebody to do something about Trump going to Fort Bragg and saying, Come on, let’s all talk about how much Joe Biden sucked.

And I said, “Where’s the Army chief of staff? Where’s Randy George?” And of course, Randy George probably—I never spoke to General George about it, but he was soon to be fired. And I think that’s the other problem with morale, is that all of these men and women are looking up the chain and saying, All the day that I do things—I was never in the military; this is something I learned from observing and talking with officers over a quarter of a century—that they look up the chain and they say, Whatever happens in politics, we have this very stable community, this very stable chain of command. People are promoted; they retire; they come up the ranks.

When Pete Hegseth inserts himself into those processes and says, All you people on this promotion list, you’re fine except for you, you, you, and you, and those four people are Black, female, disfavored groups in Hegseth’s eyes, because he thinks they were DEI hires, people start to wonder: How stable is that chain of command? What’s happening here?

And so it doesn’t surprise me at all that a lot of people would say, You know what? If I’m going to be living in a very politicized, messed-up situation where people are promoted because of politics or demoted because of how they look, I could do that and not have to wear uncomfortable boots every day.

And I think that’s really unfortunate. I think the damage to the civil-military relationship in America is a lot deeper than—we’ll realize in a few years just how much Pete Hegseth has damaged the institution of the United States military.

Youssef: You know, it’s funny: The question you were asking about the politicization of the military, it actually ties to the Iran war as well, because when you tell people that your promotion is contingent on your loyalty, politically, or your loyalty to the president or the perception [of] that, what it leads to is people less willing to give their best military advice, which they are supposed to do.

They’re not supposed to just salute and follow orders, whatever they are. They are supposed to bring forth their best military advice, and I think you saw that in the run-up to the decision to launch these strikes on Iran. So many people had been fired or demoted or pushed out—an unprecedented number—that the lesson people took was not to give their advice, but to salute even when they thought maybe the decision was less than ideal, because to do otherwise risked their jobs, and they’d seen their predecessors leave before them.

Moreover, the people who came in afterwards often had less experience than those before them because the system was not designed for this many people to be fired in this way. And so younger and younger people were coming up the chain.

The only thing I want to add—and I think it’s an important thing to note—U.S. service members do not take a personal pledge to a person or a president. They take an oath to defend the Constitution, and that is by design because we as a nation have decided we don’t want militaries loyal to any person. That has been a basic foundational principle of the United States military that begins all the way to the oath. And the more we’ve deviated from that—in many ways, the Iran war offers an example of the perils of that—that you get a military that offers different advice than it would, if it believed that it was protected.

And so back to your original question: what does Congress do? I’m curious if the Congress, both lame-duck and afterwards, starts to back some of these officers more. I think what’s been striking to me is we’ve seen so many people fired, demoted, pushed out, and, really, almost silenced from the Hill about it.

Even though these guys are signed off by the Hill, we haven’t heard anything. Are there going to be hearings in which some of these fired generals and admirals are called back? Is there going to be a public discussion about the impact of this? Because the most enduring impact Hegseth has had, in addition to the war, is on personnel. These are people with 20, 30 years experience. And then there’s all the impacts you don’t see—the captains and the majors who are looking at what’s happened to those ahead of them and saying, I’m not gonna stick around. That’s years and years of investment that has been lost, and will take years and years and years to replace.

Harris: How big of a deal would it be if Defense Secretary Hegseth were impeached?

Youssef: Well, it’d be a huge deal. We’ve only had two Cabinet secretaries in the history of the country impeached, neither one of them convicted. Certainly not the person in charge of the largest government organization, the one asking for more than a trillion dollars in government funding, the one responsible for 2 million troops and part of the chain of command.

It would be extraordinary, and an incredible condemnation of the top civilian at the Pentagon while the United States has forces deployed and a blockade happening in the Strait of Hormuz. And so it would be an unprecedented thing to happen, in many ways. But by itself, it doesn’t—I don’t think—lead to the sort of foundational questions that need to be asked and answered in terms of: What kind of Defense Department do we want, moving forward?

Nichols: It’s a huge deal because Pete Hegseth’s gonna make it a huge deal. A better secretary of defense—and by that I mean almost any secretary of defense—would say, All right, I’m impeached, but we get back to work. You know, life goes on. He would say to the troops: This is not about you. This is something happening in Washington. We’ve got this.

But two things will happen, I suspect. One is it will send a message—and I think this is necessary—from the Congress to a lot of people in the high command, the senior command of the United States, that says: Look, we haven’t forgotten that you’re doing things like extrajudicial murders of people in the Caribbean. Just because it’s off the newspapers doesn’t mean that we, the representatives and the people of the United States, have forgotten that you guys were doing this.

So that’s a salutary effect, because I think it’s been a tragedy that somehow that just went on and we said, Well, I guess that’s just the way it is.

The worst part is that Pete Hegseth will—he’s already done it. He’s going to try to drag the troops into this. These ads where he has himself posing with Stephen Miller and saying, “Stand and fight,” that’s not about the mission of the Defense Department. That’s Pete Hegseth doing an ad for himself that he’s putting out and hoping that the president sees it and doesn’t fire him, but also a message to the troops. It’s us against them. I’m your secretary of defense. These terrible civilian leaders—the ones in the Constitution that, as Nancy points out, that you’re sworn to protect—they’re the enemy now.

And so I think it’s necessary. I think it’s important that it happened. But I think that Pete Hegseth will use it to divide the troops even more than he has tried to in the past. And I think that, strangely enough, that’s a good reason to do it. Because that kind of secretary of defense should be impeached and removed.

Harris: Well, we’ll have to leave it there. Tom, Nancy, thank you so much for joining me and helping us understand this better and sharing your reporting.

Youssef: Thanks for the great conversation.

Nichols: Thank you.

Harris: That’s all for today’s show. This episode of Radio Atlantic was produced by Mike Pesoli and edited by Kevin Townsend. It was engineered by Miguel Carrascal and has original music by Rob Smierciak. Claudine Ebeid is the executive producer of podcasts, and Andrea Valdez is our managing editor.

If you like what you saw here, new episodes of Radio Atlantic drop every Monday and Thursday. You can subscribe on The Atlantic’s YouTube page, on Apple or Spotify, or wherever it is you get your podcasts. And if you want to support this work and the work of my colleagues at The Atlantic, you can subscribe to the publication at TheAtlantic.com/Listener.

Until next time, I’m Adam Harris.

title: Trump Slides Into His Lame-Duck Era
summary: This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the best in culture. Sign up for it here.When President Trump posted on Saturday that he’d asked Dana White, the head of the Ultimate Fighting C...
content:
This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the best in culture. Sign up for it here.

When President Trump posted on Saturday that he’d asked Dana White, the head of the Ultimate Fighting Championship, to be the new White House press secretary, it felt like a callback to the freewheeling first-term Trump.

“I am pleased to announce that the Great Dana White, a violent Fighter and Warrior, has been offered the job of Press Secretary of the United States,” the president wrote on Truth Social, adding that he needed White and his band of mixed-martial-arts fighters “to defend us against the Lunatic Left. Dana will be a Press Secretary like none other. Dana, please take the job!”

By weekend’s end, the possibility of the appointment had dissolved, though not without a subplot of speculation that Trump was confusing the impresario with another Dana White who had actually served as a Pentagon spokesperson during his first term. CNN reported that White had declined, and last night, Trump told reporters he never meant it anyway. “I was only kidding, but Dana loves the idea,” he said.

Perhaps. Trump has a long record of launching outlandish ideas and then playing them off as jokes when they don’t work out. If it was all a jape, then the weak stab at humor seems to underestimate the electorate’s frustration with his antics. If he was serious and got rejected, it’s even worse. An old maxim goes that when the president of the United States asks you to do something, you do it. But Trump no longer has the juice he did in the early days of this administration, when billionaire tech CEOs were showering him with attention and the odd bauble. Last Tuesday evening, as election results rolled in, my colleague Jonathan Lemire wrote that “Donald J. Trump is now officially, thoroughly a lame duck.” Now we’re getting a glimpse of what that looks like in practice.

Start with the cool reception that Trump’s elevation of Stephen Miller to White House chief of staff received among Republicans. Representative Marlin Stutzman called it a “horrible decision.” Another legislator told Fox News that his reaction was “utter disbelief.” When a Politico reporter informed one member of the choice, they replied, “Please tell me you’re lying to me right now, just to get a reaction.” Take these statements with a grain of salt—Republicans have often been happy to talk trash about Trump anonymously while going along with him publicly—but whether or not they acquiesce with the president matters less now that the GOP is so outnumbered in Congress.

One test of where House Republicans actually stand will come this week. Thomas Massie, a renegade GOP member who Trump helped defeat in a primary earlier this year, refiled articles of impeachment against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth today. Although Speaker Mike Johnson (speaking of lame ducks) had temporarily stymied Massie’s impeachment efforts in September by sending members home until after the midterms, the House is now back in session. Rounding up enough Republican votes to move the articles forward will be difficult but not impossible; a significant number of GOP members lost their seats last week, including many of the more moderate representatives, which means they are less in Trump’s thrall. Assuming that Hegseth is not impeached this month, it seems all but inevitable once Democrats take over. This weekend, presumptive Speaker Hakeem Jeffries said he’s a “hard yes” on impeachment.

Republicans’ losses have produced infighting elsewhere in the party too. As Miller moves to take over, fallout from his predecessor Susie Wiles’s tenure continues. Calley Means, a former aide to Robert F. Kennedy Jr., appeared on Joe Rogan’s podcast, where he accused Wiles and James Blair, a top Trump political adviser, of selling the MAHA movement out to corporate interests. The Wall Street Journal reports that, ahead of their public social-media fight, Blair texted Means, “If you are gonna try to knife me, I’m happy to return the favor.” Meanwhile Senator Ron Johnson, a hard-right figure from Wisconsin, has picked up on Means’s comments to accuse the Trump administration of “corruption.”

One person in particular left somewhat unmoored by the results is Vice President Vance, who built his entire profile on closeness to a politician whose toxicity is now made plain. In a long post-election X post, Vance pinned the midterm defeat on the Iran war. This was widely seen as a swipe at the president and an attempt to position himself for 2028, but as The New Yorker’s Jason Zengerle observed, Vance “didn’t so much throw Trump under the bus as try to bring him on board his bandwagon by essentially putting words in Trump’s mouth.”

But Trump does not seem inclined to cooperate. For one thing, he continues to defend the war. On 60 Minutes last night, he acknowledged the political fallout but said, “I think, historically, this will be a very good decision. Is it a good decision for today and tomorrow? Maybe not.” Speaking with reporters last night, he once again declared victory in the unresolved war with Iran and then claimed, falsely and callously, that “we haven’t lost anybody. No soldiers.”

At other times, though, Trump has sounded unusually chastened since Election Day. He told The New York Times that he looks forward to working with the Democrats. He also acknowledged on 60 Minutes that his deportation policy, which “might be too tough,” could explain the GOP’s shellacking. “I think I got an A-plus for closing up the border,” he said, “but I get hurt because we also took people that had good jobs, that created one violation, or breaking of the law, and that was that they came into the country illegally.” A deescalation on immigration enforcement seems unlikely with Miller as chief of staff, given his role in implementing that policy, but the fact that Trump was willing to offer conciliatory remarks suggests that he is beginning to recognize the challenges of life as a lame duck.

Today’s News

  1. Nvidia’s board is investigating whether the company’s CEO, Jensen Huang, shared sensitive information with an executive suspected of having ties to Chinese intelligence. This comes after Huang confirmed yesterday that he had an affair with the executive, who worked for a Singapore-based data-center company. Nvidia said it has no reason to believe any secrets were compromised.
  2. Republican Representative Thomas Massie introduced articles of impeachment against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, setting up a House vote by Wednesday. Hegseth dismissed the effort and said he agreed with President Trump’s decision to launch the war with Iran and would “do it again.”
  3. Stephen Miller, a longtime Trump adviser and the architect of the administration’s mass-deportation campaign, officially became White House chief of staff today, replacing Susie Wiles.

Evening Read

Woodward in the “Washington Post” newsroom, 1973 Paul Slade / Paris Match / Getty

The One Source Bob Woodward Can’t Get to Talk

By George Packer

Bob Woodward has published a book roughly every two years since the Watergate scandal, 24 in all. Taken together, they comprise a running narrative of almost every administration from Richard Nixon’s to Donald Trump’s. The genre of the Washington book—a sequence of scenes inside rooms where important things happen, based on a convention called “deep background,” with riches of information traced to no sources—is so familiar that it’s easy to forget that Woodward practically invented it. Decade after decade, he has kept turning up in the Oval Office, at Georgetown parties, on the doorsteps of government officials—always on the job, the hunt. His approach from across a crowded room or the sudden appearance of his name on a cellphone screen has surely sunk the heart of countless sources. And yet, though they know better, they always talk, as if transfixed by a predatory stare—like the frog that agrees to carry the scorpion on its back across the lake. “Why?” the frog cries as it drowns from the inevitable sting, to which the scorpion replies: “It’s my nature.”

title: Collision of two trains in Egypt kills at least seven

content:
President orders prompt investigation after one train derails in collision in al-Ayyat about 50km from Cairo

Seven people were killed and at least 125 injured when two trains collided on Sunday south of the Egyptian capital, Cairo, officials said.

The crash occurred in al-Ayyat district in Giza province, about 50km (30 miles) south of Cairo, when a train travelling to Fayoum province crashed into the rear of a train heading to the southern province of Aswan, according to the transport ministry.

content:
Paul Mackenzie convicted over deaths of children and one adult after followers were ordered to starve themselves and their families

The leader of a Kenyan doomsday sect has been sentenced to 200 years in prison for the murders of 190 children and one adult in one of the world’s worst cult disasters in recent history.

The sentence, comprising 100 years for murder by starvation and 100 years by direct homicide, came two weeks after the court in Kenya’s coastal city of Mombasa found the cult leader guilty of the crimes.

title: ANC faces bruising defeat in South African local elections with 80% of ballots counted
summary: Former liberation movement’s share of national vote almost 14 percentage points below 2021 resultThe African National Congress is on course to suffer a bruising defeat in South Africa’s local elections, with the once dominant party of Nelson Mandela falling to under a third of the vote nationally wi...
content:
Former liberation movement’s share of national vote almost 14 percentage points below 2021 result

The African National Congress is on course to suffer a bruising defeat in South Africa’s local elections, with the once dominant party of Nelson Mandela falling to under a third of the vote nationally with more than 80% of ballots counted.

Wednesday’s fragmented vote marks another stage in the decline of the ANC, which has led national governments since the end of white minority apartheid rule in 1994. High unemployment, crime, corruption and poor local service delivery have all contributed to voters turning away from the party.

“A British citizen currently in the DR Congo has tested positive for Ebola,” a spokesperson for the UK government said in a statement on Wednesday. “The UK has well-established procedures for dealing with cases like this, and those processes have been activated … The risk to the UK public from Ebola remains low.”
